idiom_name: iter.Seq[T] = func(yield func(T) bool), driven by for range
implementation_notes: Since Go 1.23 an iterator is any function taking a yield callback, wrapped as iter.Seq[T] and driven by for range: the loop that advances the seed is the unfold, the state lives in locals, and early termination is yield returning false. It is the language-blessed form - no goroutine, no channel and no leak when the consumer stops early - so prefer it over the channel generator whenever the toolchain allows.
pitfalls: yield's bool result must be checked: ignoring it keeps generating after the consumer stopped and can spin forever.
The iterator body runs inside the consumer's range loop, so a panic, a blocking call or a long step is paid on the consumer's goroutine and stack.
A nested loop cannot yield directly unless the nested function has the same signature; iteration must be flattened or delegated to another iter.Seq.

variants.name: Goroutine producer feeding a channel (pre-1.23)
variants.idiom_name: go func() { out <- layer }() with defer close(out)
variants.implementation_notes: The classic Go generator: a goroutine owns the seed, sends each produced layer on an unbuffered channel and closes it when the step function stops, while the consumer ranges over the channel. It runs the producer concurrently and blocks naturally on a slow consumer, but the goroutine survives an early exit unless the consumer drains the channel or a done channel/context is selected on.
pitfalls: A consumer that stops ranging early leaves the producer blocked on send forever: select on a done channel or cancel a context.
One goroutine plus channel per unfold is far heavier than the range-over-func form; use it only when the producer must run concurrently or block on I/O.
